## Conclusion: The evidence largely supports "no" — probiotics do not reliably shorten acute infectious diarrhea

Your skepticism is well-founded and matches the best current evidence, though the picture has evolved over time and remains somewhat mixed depending on study quality.

**Older, smaller meta-analyses suggested a modest benefit.** Earlier pooled analyses (e.g., in children) reported that probiotics reduced diarrhea duration by roughly 1 day. These findings underpinned earlier clinical guidance favoring probiotic use.

**However, the highest-quality, most recent evidence overturns this.** The updated 2020 Cochrane systematic review (Collinson et al.), which incorporated large, rigorous, well-designed trials, concluded that "probiotics may not affect how long acute diarrhoea lasts" and found no significant difference in diarrhea lasting ≥48 hours or ≥14 days between probiotic and control groups. The review authors specifically note that when only trials at low risk of bias were considered, the apparent benefit seen in older analyses disappeared (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD003048.pub4/full; https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea).

**This is corroborated by two large, well-powered, multicenter randomized trials published in 2018 in the New England Journal of Medicine.** Schnadower et al. tested Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG in nearly 1,000 children with acute gastroenteritis in U.S. emergency departments, and Freedman et al. conducted a similar Canadian trial. Both found no significant difference in outcomes (including diarrhea duration/severity) between probiotic and placebo groups (https://www.nih.gov/news-events/nih-research-matters/probiotics-not-helpful-young-children-diarrhea).

**Bottom line:** While earlier, smaller studies suggested modest benefit, the largest and most rigorous trials and the updated Cochrane review show probiotics likely do not meaningfully shorten acute infectious diarrhea — the earlier positive signal appears attributable to bias in smaller/lower-quality studies.
